title: Why You Shouldn't Ask Students “The Five Questions”
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin critiques a discipline strategy adopted by several school districts, in which a teacher responds to a rule violation by asking a misbehaving student a scripted sequence of five accountability questions built around the idea of a classroom 'social contract.' He identifies three problems: it costs valuable instructional time to pause a lesson and pull a student aside for the exchange; it creates antagonistic friction, since being interrogated feels like the third degree even when the questions aren't intended to sound angry, and students often answer just to end the encounter; and it produces forced compliance rather than genuine reflection, since real behavior change requires a student to choose to reflect on their own rather than being compelled to perform it verbally. His alternative is a pre-taught, clearly explained set of rules enforced dispassionately, without questioning, so students are left to reflect and choose differently on their own.
points: The critiqued strategy, 'the five questions,' has been adopted by a number of school districts as a response to rule violations.
Problem one is time cost: pausing a lesson to question a student sacrifices valuable instructional minutes.
Problem two is friction: being interrogated feels antagonistic even when questions aren't meant to sound angry, breeding resentment.
Problem three is that forced verbal compliance isn't genuine reflection; real change requires a student to choose to reflect independently.
The recommended alternative is dispassionate enforcement of pre-taught rules without questioning, letting students reflect on their own.
quotes: There is a classroom management strategy called “the five questions” that a number of school districts have adopted.
To stop whatever you’re doing—pausing in the middle of a lesson, for example—to approach a student or pull them aside isn’t realistic.
Questioning a misbehaving student is antagonistic. From the student’s viewpoint it feels like the third degree.
Forced reflection isn’t reflection at all. For actual change in behavior, a student must decide to turn from their ways of their own volition.
By any other name, the five questions are an excruciating consequence that merely show a teacher’s dominance.
A much better approach is to have a set of rules that you create in order to protect learning, your likability, and your students’ love for being in your classroom.
